narrative:
The model estimated a 52.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure slightly more likely than passing, and that risk level led to denial of your law school application.

The decision was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward bar failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the next most influential factor. At 3.10 it was below the accepted-student average of about 3.23, but its influence actually pushed toward passing rather than failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor: you were in the third decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, and this again pushed toward failure. So the model saw real academic strength in your GPA, but your lower class standing in the first and third years weighed more heavily.

To move forward, ask the admissions office for specific feedback, then build a concrete academic-improvement plan. If you reapply, focus on raising your upper-year academic standing, consider admissions test preparation or a retake, and seek advising on bar-exam readiness and study skills. Use this result as a planning signal, not a final judgment.
